newsitem.title: USA: Allegheny Power to buy Pittsburgh utility DQE.
newsitem.headline: Allegheny Power to buy Pittsburgh utility DQE.

text.p: Allegheny Power Systems Inc., an electric utility serving five eastern states, will acquire Pittsburgh area utility DQE Inc. for $2.6 billion, the companies said Monday.

The company, which will be renamed Allegheny Energy, will have more than 2 million customers, combining the mostly rural operations of Allegheny with the urban-dominated operations of DQE. Its headquarters will be near Hagerstown, Md.
DQE is the parent company of Duquesne Light Co., which has 580,000 customers in an area of 800 square miles in and around Pittsburgh.
Allegheny, based in Hagerstown, has 1.4 million customers in parts of Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia and West Virginia.

Under terms of the transaction, DQE shareholders will receive 1.12 shares of Allegheny Power for each share of DQE. Allegheny said it will issue about 86.5 million shares to DQE shareholders, which, based on Friday's closing prices, makes the deal worth $2.6 billion.
Also based on that price, each DQE share would be worth $33.32. Allegheny closed Friday at $29.75 and DQE closed at $27.125, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
In afternoon trading Monday, DQE climbed $1.75 to $28.875 and Allegheny fell 87.5 cents to $28.875.
Alan Noia, chief executive officer of Allegheny Power, will be chairman of the new company, and David Marshall, president of DQE, will be president.
Analysts praised the deal because it would give the combined company a more favourable customer mix, save costs and likely keep a lid on future rate increases.
"I think it's an excellent fit ... there is geographic proximity and complementary features, including customer mix," said Barry Abramson at Prudential Securities.

"Allegheny is primarily rural, DQE is urban. DQE's mix has a small industrial component to it and Allegheny's has a large one. I think there will be rate decreases as the companies work out a plan to pass through their savings."

The companies said they expected to achieve merger-related savings of about $1 billion over the next 10 years and utility rates should be less expensive than they would be if the companies remained separate.
The companies said about 500 jobs would be lost as a result of the merger, achieved primarily through attrition and early retirements. The combined workforce is expected to be about 8,500.
The merger is conditioned on approval by shareholders of both companies and by state and federal regulators. The companies said they hope to receive all necessary approvals within 12 to 18 months.
